original_goal_and_notes.item: Zorn's lemma: statement, proof from AC, equivalence noted
original_goal_and_notes.notes: absent book-wide; felt at 3978 where it is the standard tool for Henkin--Lindenbaum; cross-cutting list (Zorn/AC-equivalents)

required_components: State Zorn's maximal-element principle with its poset/chain hypotheses.
Supply the complete derivation from the Axiom of Choice.
State and link the equivalence with well-ordering/Choice without treating the equivalence note as the whole AC-equivalence package.

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-ac-to-zorn}{proved=annex:p6.choice.1}{Choice implies Zorn's lemma}
Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{AC}\).  If every chain in a poset \(P\),
including the empty chain, has an upper bound in \(P\), then \(P\) has a
maximal element.  The proof uses the well-order of \(P\), transfinite
recursion on the set ordinal \(h(P)\), Replacement for the range at each
stage, and Hartogs's theorem.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p6.choice.1}{thm:p06-ac-to-zorn}{Choice implies Zorn's lemma}
\begin{proof}
Work in \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{AC}\).  Let \((P,\leq)\) satisfy the chain
hypothesis.  The empty chain has an upper bound, so \(P\ne\varnothing\).
Fix \(p_*\in P\).  By the well-ordering clause of
Theorem~\ref{thm:p06-choice-equivalents-source}, fix a well-order
\(\triangleleft\) of \(P\).  Write \(x<y\) for
\(x\leq y\land x\ne y\), and let \(h(P)\) be the Hartogs ordinal of \(P\).

Use transfinite recursion on the set ordinal \(h(P)\) to construct pairs
\((a_\alpha,x_\alpha)\in\{0,1\}\times P\).  Suppose the earlier pairs have
been constructed.  If every earlier flag is \(1\) and the set
\[
  C_\alpha=\{x_\beta:\beta<\alpha\}
\]
has a strict upper bound in \(P\), set \(a_\alpha=1\) and let
\(x_\alpha\) be the \(\triangleleft\)-least strict upper bound of
\(C_\alpha\).  Otherwise set \(a_\alpha=0\) and
\(x_\alpha=p_*\).  The defining operation is single-valued.  At each stage
Replacement collects the earlier pairs and their second coordinates, so
\(C_\alpha\) is a set; Separation forms the set of its strict upper bounds,
and the fixed well-order selects its least member.  Thus the set-recursion
theorem supplies the sequence on all of \(h(P)\).

If every flag were \(1\), then for \(\beta<\alpha<h(P)\) the element
\(x_\alpha\) would be strictly above \(x_\beta\).  Hence
\(\alpha\mapsto x_\alpha\) would be an injection \(h(P)\to P\),
contrary to Hartogs's theorem.  Let \(\alpha<h(P)\) be the least stage with
\(a_\alpha=0\).  Every earlier flag is \(1\), so \(C_\alpha\) is a chain,
and the definition of the stopping stage says that it has no strict upper
bound.  (The stage is nonzero because every member of nonempty \(P\) is a
strict upper bound of the empty chain.)

By hypothesis, \(C_\alpha\) has an upper bound \(u\in P\).  If
\(u\notin C_\alpha\), then every \(c\in C_\alpha\) satisfies
\(c<u\), making \(u\) a strict upper bound.  Therefore
\(u\in C_\alpha\) and it is the greatest member of that chain.  If some
\(y\in P\) satisfied \(u<y\), then transitivity would make \(y\) a strict
upper bound of all of \(C_\alpha\), again impossible.  Thus no element of
\(P\) lies strictly above \(u\), so \(u\) is maximal.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-arbitrary-prop-compactness-bpi}{cited=HowardRubin1998}{Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem and unrestricted propositional compactness}
Working over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (equivalently,
the Ultrafilter Lemma of Definition~\ref{def:ultrafilter-lemma}) is equivalent
to the following scheme: for every set \(P\) of propositional variables and
every set \(\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Form}(P)\), if each finite subset
of \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable, then \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.
\end{hbtheorem}

original_goal_and_notes.item: Countable choice: statement, status, and where the book uses it
original_goal_and_notes.notes: raised in an exercise, resolved nowhere

required_components: State countable Choice and distinguish it from finite Choice, dependent Choice and full AC.
Record the exact implication/nonimplication status under the stated metatheory.
Identify every actual use in the current book, with a named dependency or an explicit stronger/weaker principle actually used.

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p06-countable-dependent-choice}{Countable Choice and Dependent Choice}
The \emph{Axiom of Countable Choice}, \(\mathsf{AC}_{\omega}\), says that
for every sequence \(\langle X_n:n\in\N\rangle\) of nonempty sets there is
a function \(f:\N\to\bigcup_{n\in\N}X_n\) with \(f(n)\in X_n\) for every
\(n\).  Its restriction to sequences of nonempty finite sets is the
\emph{Axiom of Countable Choice for finite sets},
\(\mathsf{AC}_{\omega}^{\mathrm{fin}}\).  The \emph{Axiom of Dependent
Choice}, \(\mathsf{DC}\), says that whenever \(X\) is nonempty,
\(R\subseteq X\times X\) is serial, and \(x_0\in X\), there is a sequence
\(\langle x_n:n\in\N\rangle\) beginning with \(x_0\) and satisfying
\(x_nRx_{n+1}\) for every \(n\).
These are metatheoretic principles about constructing sequences, not rules of
any object-language calculus.  Dependent Choice is stronger because its next
choice may depend on the preceding value; this distinction is needed in the
dependency table.
\index{Axiom of Countable Choice}
\index{Axiom of Countable Choice!for finite sets}
\index{Dependent Choice}
\end{hbdefinition}
